OriginalPhrase: On the primary test
Before: Federated learning trains a shared model without pooling raw electronic health record (EHR) access logs. The server can still inspect individual model updates. This study compared detection performance and training cost with and without secure aggregation of those updates. It evaluated pooled centralised training, standard Federated Averaging and Federated Averaging with Secure Aggregation Plus (SecAgg+) using a long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder, a model that learns to reconstruct routine access sequences. Experiments used one supplied benchmark described as synthetic, three simulated clients and five random seeds. Sampling either retained the original client distributions or favoured selected departments. On the primary test, the mean paired differences in global average precision, a measure of threat ranking, between SecAgg+ and standard Federated Averaging were +0.0047 and +0.0001 in the two sampling conditions. These differences did not establish equivalent performance. Federated training did not consistently outperform pooled training. Compared with standard Federated Averaging, SecAgg+ increased the time recorded for the training workflow by 132.8% and 128.6%, respectively. The content carried in application messages increased by approximately 49.9%. All configurations struggled with unusual legitimate activity. For SecAgg+, mean false-positive rates were 98.58% and 96.40% on the secondary test. Repeating the experiment in a fresh software environment on the same computer reproduced the predictions, with a disclosed exception in scaler metadata. Protected aggregation therefore added workflow cost without a clear detection benefit in this benchmark. Protection depended on a trusted host and honest participants. Incomplete records of data generation and the use of simulated clients limit what the findings imply for hospitals.

Section: 2.1 EHR access security and audit logs
OriginalPhrase: They combined positive examples from the intervention sample with negative examples borrowed from the control sample.
Before: Early detection studies learnt from examples reviewed by privacy officers. Boxwala et al. (2011) used logistic regression to estimate class probabilities and support vector machines (SVMs) to learn a boundary between classes. Their training labels marked accesses as suspicious or appropriate, rather than confirming incident outcomes. Kim et al. (2011) used anomaly and signature filtering to select examples for logistic regression. They combined positive examples from the intervention sample with negative examples borrowed from the control sample. The external tests included only inappropriate accesses: independently investigated cases for Boxwala et al. and independently identified cases for Kim et al. After: Early detection studies used examples reviewed by privacy officers. Boxwala et al. Section: 2.4 Secure aggregation of federated model updates
OriginalPhrase: If the server has the stated knowledge of the input distribution
Before: A combined update can still disclose information under some threat models. In an arXiv preprint, Ngo et al. (2024) analyse a passive server that observes the protocol without changing it. If the server has the stated knowledge of the input distribution, it can use aggregate updates to distinguish between candidate client inputs. This differs from directly inspecting an individual update. Evaluations should therefore report protocol assumptions and visible outputs alongside utility and cost. Claims about protection during aggregation must remain separate from claims about privacy across the whole monitoring system.
After: A combined update can still disclose information under some threat models. In an arXiv preprint, Ngo et al. (2024) analyse a passive server that follows the protocol and observes the exact sum of client updates. It is assumed able to simulate training to sample client updates and estimate their averages and how entries vary together. Given two candidate updates, these estimates and the aggregate may help identify which candidate a client submitted. This is statistical inference rather than direct inspection of an individual update. Evaluations should report protocol assumptions and visible outputs with utility and cost. Protection during aggregation does not establish privacy across the whole monitoring system.
